---
name: code-review
description: Review pull requests for supply-chain risk by inspecting the actual code behind dependency, plugin, action, toolchain, and image updates.
---

# Code review

## Security objective

The primary goal of this review is to prevent supply-chain compromise. Automated
dependency updates are untrusted until the code between the pinned old and new
revisions has been inspected. A local diff that changes only a version, hash, or
lockfile entry represents all upstream code introduced by that revision range.

Look for both intentionally malicious behavior and security-relevant behavior
that may be legitimate upstream but unsafe in this repository. Do not treat an
established project, trusted maintainer, signed commit, automated update, passing
CI, or small local diff as proof that an update is safe.

## General PR review

- When reviewing pull requests, do not rely only on the PR title, labels, or autogenerated dependency bump message.
- Inspect the actual code that will become trusted and describe likely behavior,
  tooling, security, and compatibility impact.

## Dependency, lockfile, plugin, and vendored updates

Review the actual dependency changes, not just the bumped versions.

When the repository diff only shows a version, SHA, or lockfile entry change:

1. Identify every bumped dependency and its upstream repository from the
   lockfile, package metadata, local configuration, or links in the PR.
2. Open the upstream comparison from the exact old revision to the exact new
   revision.
3. Inspect the patch for every commit in that range. Commit messages, a commit
   list, release notes, changelogs, tags, and generated PR comments help locate
   changes, but are not substitutes for reading the changed code and
   configuration.
4. Inspect added and modified executable code, build and release configuration,
   generated artifacts, dependency metadata, and tests. Tests can reveal intended
   behavior but do not make the corresponding runtime change safe.
5. Summarize the behavior introduced by those commits, especially changed
   defaults, APIs, commands, configuration keys, generated files, runtime
   requirements, and transitive dependencies.
6. Connect each relevant upstream change to the local files and workflows that
   use the dependency. Inspect those local call sites or configuration paths
   before deciding whether the change is safe.
7. Inspect the complete repository at the proposed PR head, not only the base
   checkout plus isolated diffs. Check out the proposed revision in a detached
   worktree when possible, or inspect an equivalent immutable snapshot. Evaluate
   the updated dependency together with the exact Neovim configuration, plugin
   declarations, lockfile, startup code, commands, mappings, and automation that
   would use it after merge.

Treat the proposed checkout as untrusted. Inspect the relevant code before
executing it, then use dynamic checks when they can reveal behavior that static
inspection cannot. A disposable GitHub-hosted environment is suitable only when
the process has no secrets, personal files, writable host paths, privileged or
write-capable GitHub token, or ability to publish caches, artifacts, packages,
releases, or repository changes. Use temporary `HOME` and XDG directories and
restrict network access when the check does not require it.

When those conditions hold, run focused checks such as starting Neovim headless
with the proposed configuration and exercising locally used plugin paths. Do not
run unrelated repository scripts, installers, or update hooks. Record the exact
commands, environment constraints, observed behavior, and any checks skipped for
safety. Successful execution supplements code inspection; it does not establish
that an update is free of dormant or environment-dependent malicious behavior.

Specifically investigate changes that:

- execute shell commands, downloaded code, package-manager lifecycle scripts,
  native binaries, dynamic modules, or code assembled at runtime
- add or change network requests, download locations, update channels, mirrors,
  registries, Git remotes, submodules, or integrity verification
- read or transmit credentials, tokens, environment variables, editor buffers,
  SSH or GPG material, browser data, configuration, or other local files
- alter authentication, authorization, signature or checksum checks, sandboxing,
  path validation, permissions, workflow permissions, or trust boundaries
- write outside expected cache or data directories, modify startup files, add
  persistence, invoke privileged operations, or change executable search paths
- introduce obfuscated, minified, encoded, generated, vendored, or binary content
  whose behavior cannot be established from the reviewed patch
- add dependencies or move behavior into transitive dependencies that are not
  pinned or whose introduced code has not been inspected

For each such change, determine whether the local configuration can reach it,
what data and privileges it receives, and whether the behavior is necessary and
appropriately constrained. Report plausible exploit paths and security boundary
changes as findings even when the upstream change appears intentional. Evaluate
the effective merged behavior, including interactions between otherwise benign
upstream changes and local configuration.

Do not stop after reading the local lockfile diff or an automated comment that
lists upstream commit subjects. Do not infer that a commit is irrelevant from
its subject alone; inspect its patch first. Release notes and changelogs are
secondary context after the exact commit range has been reviewed.

If the upstream repository or any commit patch is unavailable, identify the
dependency and uninspected revision range explicitly. Treat that as incomplete
review coverage instead of concluding that the version bump has no issues. Do
not recommend approval while introduced executable code or security-relevant
configuration remains uninspected.

Check for impact on:

- shell functions, scripts, and editor tooling behavior
- configuration compatibility across fish, neovim, sway, waybar, and related tools
- transitive dependency changes and hidden defaults
- major version jumps, deprecations, and changed error behavior
- security-sensitive paths such as auth, tokens, remote fetches, and command execution

Do not approve only because the PR is autogenerated, the bump looks small, the
local diff is only a lockfile/version/hash update, an upstream commit list looks
routine, or CI passes.

In the review summary, list each dependency's exact old and new revisions, the
upstream commits whose patches were inspected, the behavior changes found, the
proposed revision or snapshot inspected, the relevant local paths inspected, and
any uninspected commits or remaining validation needs. State whether any new code
can execute commands, access local data or credentials, communicate over the
network, change trust checks, or introduce further unreviewed code.

## CI, GitHub Actions, toolchain, container image, and packaging updates

Review the effective change, not just the version or SHA update.

Check for impact on:

- workflow permissions and token usage
- defaults, inputs, deprecated behavior, and runner compatibility
- test reliability and coverage
- release automation, artifact handling, and reproducibility
- cache behavior and platform-specific execution

Do not approve only because the change is in workflows, is SHA-pinned, or CI passes.

In the review summary, state what changed, what was inspected, and any remaining risk or recommended verification.
